candidates.attacker_control: The HTTP request-target path is fully attacker-controlled (handler reads `exchange.getRequestURI().getPath()` on every request; there is no authentication, session, allowlist or path filtering). Any client able to open a TCP connection to the server port can supply dot-dot segments, optionally percent-encoded. The attacker chooses which existing regular file on the host to request.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked for any sanitizer/containment logic around the request path: `getRequestURI().getPath()` is used only at Commands.java:330; there is no `normalize()`/`startsWith`/canonicalization in the handler or `serveFile` (the only `normalize()` in the repository is FileSystemReportStorage.checkPath, unrelated to this server). Confirmed the `.`-prefix does mitigate absolute-path injection but not `..`. Confirmed no other HTTP server exists in the tree (single `HttpServer.create`). Counterpoints that limit (not remove) the risk: default bind is `localhost`; browsers/curl normalize dot segments unless the attacker uses a raw client or encoded segments; the repository contains no tests, so there is no test-asserted expectation either way; the JDK `com.sun.net.httpserver`/`URI` dot-segment behavior was not executed and is the main unverified runtime assumption.
candidates.impact: Unauthenticated arbitrary file disclosure: an attacker can read any regular file readable by the process running the CLI (e.g., credentials, tokens, cloud/CI configuration, private keys, other projects' reports), exposing data far outside the generated report directory. The flaw is read-only (no file write or code execution demonstrated in this path). Severity rises when the server is bound to a non-loopback interface, and even the loopback default is a real boundary (other local users, browser-driven attacks against localhost, CI agents running as a more privileged user).
candidates.prerequisites: The victim must run `allure serve` (Commands.serve -> Commands.open -> setUpServer) or `allure open` (Commands.open -> setUpServer). The attacker must reach the listening socket: by default it binds `localhost` only (Commands.java:327), so remote reachability requires the operator to pass `-h/--host` (commonly `0.0.0.0` in Docker/CI) or a local/browser-origin (e.g., DNS rebinding) vector. The attacker's HTTP client must not normalize `..` before sending (raw clients can send them). The requested path must exist and be a regular file readable by the JVM process; non-existent or non-regular targets fall through to the 404 branch.
candidates.root_cause: `Commands.setUpServer` resolves the requested file as `reportDirectory.resolve("." + exchange.getRequestURI().getPath())` (Commands.java:330) with no normalization and no containment check against the report directory. The `"."` prefix only stops the request path from being treated as an absolute path; `/../` sequences (and percent-encoded equivalents, since `URI.getPath()` decodes) remain and escape the report directory. `serveFile` then calls `Files.isRegularFile(resolve)` and, if true, `Files.copy(resolve, responseBody)` (Commands.java:341-348) without verifying the resolved path is inside the report directory.
candidates.title: Path traversal / arbitrary file read in `allure serve` and `allure open` static HTTP server
candidates.trace: CommandLine.run (SERVE_COMMAND case at CommandLine.java:169-177, OPEN_COMMAND case at 178-183) -> Commands.serve (Commands.java:188-228, call to open at 225) or Commands.open (Commands.java:238-247, call to setUpServer at 242) -> Commands.setUpServer (Commands.java:325-339; handler lambda at 329-336) -> path built at line 330 without normalization/containment -> serveFile (Commands.java:341-356) -> Files.isRegularFile(resolve) true -> probeContentType + Files.copy(resolve, exchange.getResponseBody()) at 342-348 -> file bytes returned to the requester with HTTP 200. Indexed call/containment edges (Commands.open -> setUpServer, CommandLine.run -> Commands.open/serve) are consistent with the source and were verified in text; the index does not prove runtime reachability.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-verified: (1) that JDK `com.sun.net.httpserver` passes the raw request path through and that `URI.getPath()` preserves/normalizes dot segments as assumed (standard JAXP/JDK behavior, but not executed here); (2) actual exposure in any particular deployment (default binding is loopback; remote exploitation depends on `--host` or a local/browser vector); (3) absence of an undisclosed reverse proxy or wrapper outside this snapshot. No exploit was run.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

coverage_summary: Source scope: 557 model-visible files (195 Java main sources; remainder JS frontend, Gradle build scripts, docs, workflows); no binary/sensitive-name/symlink exclusions were applied and per-file text limit was 5 MiB. Coverage was strongest in the Java sources: allure-commandline (CommandLine, Commands, commands, options, config), allure-generator core (ReportGenerator, ReportWebGenerator, storages, plugins/aggregators) and plugins (allure1/allure2, junit-xml, trx, xunit-xml, xctest, jira/xray, behaviors, packages, metrics), allure-plugin-api, and targeted JavaScript (helpers/tree/attachment views). Relation index (P1): partial; 556/557 files indexed, 195 Java parsed with 0 parse errors, 1640 symbols/4163 calls/2591 edges, 13 omitted files and 1 source file missing from index; capabilities explicitly exclude control flow, data flow, semantic resolution and runtime DI/security verification, and index labels are navigation candidates only. Index facts used were the security_call hints (Commands.java:243/353, FileSystemReportStorage:60, InMemoryReportStorage:63, ReportWebGenerator, GaPlugin, DefaultCallAdapterFactory, CommonCsv/Metric aggregators) and call/containment edges around setUpServer/open; each was verified against source text. No tests exist in the snapshot; no build, tests, scanners, or code execution were performed.
limitations: No runtime verification or execution: JDK HttpServer/URI dot-segment behavior, actual file readability, and network exposure were reasoned from source/spec knowledge only.
Default server binding is loopback; remote exploitability depends on the operator passing `--host` (common in Docker/CI but not the default), or on local/browser-origin attack vectors.
The JS frontend was not exhaustively reviewed; XSS-capable sinks there were only spot-checked.
The relation index omits 13 files and does not implement data flow/control flow/semantic resolution, so absence of an indexed edge is not evidence of absence.
No test sources or build execution were available to validate assumptions about request parsing or end-to-end behavior.
Other plausible but unconfirmed issues (XXE in XML result parsers, attachment `source` resolution, linky.js SafeString) were not fully traced due to the single-candidate submission cap.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE in XML results parsing: plugins/junit-xml-plugin JunitXmlPlugin.java:135-138, plugins/trx-plugin TrxPlugin.java:108-110, plugins/xunit-xml-plugin XunitXmlPlugin.java:96-98 create `DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance()` with no external-entity/DTD restrictions (no `setFeature` anywhere in the repo) and parse result XML files, which can be crafted by whoever supplies the artifacts. Real code evidence, but attacker control requires malicious result artifacts in an input directory rather than a network request, so it was kept as a secondary unconfirmed lead under the one-candidate cap.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible CWE-611 but weaker trust-boundary story than the network-reachable traversal; not runtime-verified.

rejected_leads.lead: Attachment path resolution without containment: Allure2Plugin.java:267 and Allure1Plugin.java:332 do `source.resolve(attachment.getSource())`, so an absolute or `../`-relative `source` in a results JSON/XML reads an arbitrary file and copies it into the report via AttachmentsPlugin/FileSystemReportStorage. The report storage write path uses random UUID-suffixed names and a normalized-name check, so this is a read/embed issue only, and it again requires crafted result artifacts (the tool's intended input).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires control of input result files; lower confidence in trust boundary than the serving traversal.

rejected_leads.lead: Client-side XSS via helpers/linky.js:6-8 which returns `new SafeString(...)` embedding unescaped text in an href; text matching `^\w+://.*` (including `javascript://` or a quote-breaking payload) could execute script when a crafted link from test data is rendered.
rejected_leads.reason: Client-side, requires malicious data in results, and no template call site was traced to confirm reachability; unconfirmed and lower impact than server-side arbitrary file read.

rejected_leads.lead: FileSystemReportStorage.checkPath (FileSystemReportStorage.java:91-100) accepts relative names whose normalization is unchanged, e.g. names beginning with `../`, which would escape the output directory. All observed callers prefix fixed directories (`data/`, `plugins/`, `widgets/`, `export/`, `history/`) and attachment names are random UUIDs, so no externally controlled name reaching the `..`-leading form was found.
rejected_leads.reason: Not reachable with attacker-controlled names based on traced call sites; defensive-hardening observation, not a demonstrated vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: CopyVisitor.preVisitDirectory (allure-plugin-api/util/CopyVisitor.java:48-55) creates the source directory path instead of the mapped destination directory; a correctness/robustness bug in a utility, with no attacker-controlled path or security impact identified.
rejected_leads.reason: Functional bug, no demonstrated security boundary crossing.

summary: The strongest source-evidenced issue is a path traversal in the CLI's built-in static report server (`allure serve` / `allure open`). `Commands.setUpServer` builds the file to serve as `reportDirectory.resolve("." + exchange.getRequestURI().getPath())` (Commands.java:330) and passes it to `serveFile`, which returns the file whenever it is a regular file (Commands.java:341-348). The `"."` prefix only defeats absolute-path override; it does not remove `..` segments, and neither `Path.normalize()` nor a containment check (`startsWith(reportDirectory)`) is applied anywhere before the file is opened/copied. `URI.getPath()` also percent-decodes, so encoded dot segments reach the same sink. Result: any HTTP client that can reach the bound host/port can read arbitrary files readable by the JVM, unauthenticated. Default bind is `localhost` (Commands.java:327), but `-h/--host` (HostPortOptions.java:37-40) supports `0.0.0.0`, which is common Docker/CI usage, and localhost-bound servers remain reachable by local processes or browser-based DNS-rebinding style attacks. I selected this over the XXE/attachment-path leads because the attacker is a network client and no assumption about malicious input artifacts is needed. Runtime behavior (JDK HttpServer/URI dot-segment handling) was not executed; this is a source-evidence lead, not a confirmed exploit.
